data.name: Setup_Sub_Compat
data.value: NitroDrop can prepare your Wi-Fi card for the direct connection AirDrop uses. It takes a few steps and two restarts. We explain each step before it happens, and nothing changes until you approve it.

data.name: Setup_Sub_Unsupported
data.value: For now, the NitroDrop Wi-Fi driver only works with the Intel Wi-Fi 6 AX203 card, and this PC doesn't have one. Sharing with devices on the same network still works. We're working on support for USB Wi-Fi adapters that need no setup.

data.name: Setup_Sub_Consent
data.value: All of this is temporary: undo it with one click in Settings → Wi-Fi driver → “Uninstall”.

data.name: Setup_Sub_BitLockerOn
data.value: Your drive is encrypted with BitLocker. Changing Secure Boot can make your PC ask for the 48-digit recovery key at startup. Without the key you can't reach your files — back it up before you continue.

data.name: Setup_Sub_BitLockerUnknown
data.value: Couldn't read the BitLocker status. To be sure, run a detailed check (administrator permission required).

data.name: Setup_Sub_BitLockerNone
data.value: Your drive isn't protected by BitLocker, so there's nothing to do in this step.

data.name: Setup_Sub_SecureBootOn
data.value: Here are the steps for your {0}. When you click “Restart to BIOS”, the PC opens the BIOS settings directly — taking a photo of the steps with your phone makes it easier. Setup picks up where it left off when Windows starts.

data.name: Setup_Sub_SecureBootOff
data.value: This step is done.

data.name: Setup_Sub_SecureBootNone
data.value: Your PC may be starting in legacy (Legacy/CSM) mode; in that case Secure Boot is already disabled.

data.name: Setup_Sub_TestModeOn
data.value: Windows can now load the drivers we sign ourselves.

data.name: Setup_Sub_TestModePending
data.value: Test Mode is turned on — restart your PC for it to take effect. Setup continues where it left off when Windows starts.

data.name: Setup_Sub_TestModeEnable
data.value: Test Mode lets Windows load the driver we sign on this PC. You'll be asked for administrator permission once, then the PC restarts.

data.name: Setup_Sub_Install
data.value: Intel's Wi-Fi firmware is downloaded (from the linux-firmware repository) and verified with SHA-256; the driver is signed with a certificate unique to this PC and installed on your Wi-Fi card.

data.name: Setup_Sub_Done
data.value: Your Wi-Fi card now runs the NitroDrop driver. When nearby iPhones, iPads and Macs show up, you can share with them directly. This driver is experimental — if anything goes wrong, you can undo it with one click.

data.name: Setup_Sub_Rollback
data.value: Removes the NitroDrop driver and puts everything back the way it was before setup. You'll be asked for administrator permission once.

data.name: Setup_Sub_RollbackFailed
data.value: Details are in the setup log. You can try again, or pick the Intel driver manually in Device Manager.

data.name: Setup_Sub_RollbackRestored
data.value: The driver is removed and Test Mode is off. Restart your PC to make the watermark go away.

data.name: Setup_Sub_RollbackAlmost
data.value: One last step: turn Secure Boot back on. Click “Restart to BIOS” and follow the steps below.

data.name: Setup_Consent3_Body

data.name: Setup_Consent5_Body

data.value: Save and exit with F10 (Save & Exit). Windows starts normally and the “Test Mode” watermark is gone.

data.name: Vendor_ThinkPad_Keys
data.value: press F1 at startup (ThinkBook: F2), or Enter → F1

data.name: Vendor_ThinkPad_Step1
data.value: Use the arrow keys to go to the “Security” tab.

data.name: Vendor_ThinkPad_Step2
data.value: Open the “Secure Boot” item (Enter).

data.name: Vendor_ThinkPad_Step3
data.value: Set “Secure Boot” to “Off” / “Disabled”.

data.name: Vendor_ThinkPad_Note
data.value: If it asks for a supervisor password, enter that first.

data.name: Vendor_Lenovo_Keys
data.value: press F2 or Fn+F2 at startup; if that doesn't work, with the PC off press the Novo pinhole on the side with a pin and choose “BIOS Setup”

data.name: Vendor_Lenovo_Step1
data.value: Go to the “Security” tab at the top (on Legion, open “More Settings” first if needed).

data.name: Vendor_Lenovo_Step2
data.value: Set “Secure Boot” to “Disabled”.

data.name: Vendor_Hp_Keys
data.value: press Esc repeatedly at startup, then F10 (BIOS Setup) in the menu

data.name: Vendor_Hp_Menu
data.value: System Configuration (or Advanced) → Boot Options / Secure Boot Configuration

data.name: Vendor_Hp_Step1
data.value: On the “System Configuration” tab, open “Boot Options” (business models: “Advanced” → “Secure Boot Configuration”).

data.name: Vendor_Hp_Step2
data.value: Clear the “Secure Boot” box / choose “Disable”. Leave “Legacy Support” off.

data.name: Vendor_Hp_Step4
data.value: At startup HP shows a 4-digit confirmation code and asks you to type it: enter the code on screen and press Enter. This is normal.

data.name: Vendor_Dell_Keys
data.value: press F2 at the Dell logo

data.name: Vendor_Dell_Menu
data.value: Boot Configuration → Secure Boot (older BIOS: Secure Boot → Secure Boot Enable)

data.name: Vendor_Dell_Step1
data.value: Open “Boot Configuration” in the menu on the left (older layout: “Secure Boot” → “Secure Boot Enable”).

data.name: Vendor_Dell_Step2
data.value: Turn off the “Enable Secure Boot” switch and answer “Yes” to the warning.

data.name: Vendor_Dell_Step3
data.value: Click “Apply Changes” (or “Apply”), then “Exit”. The PC restarts.

data.name: Vendor_Asus_Step1

data.name: Vendor_Asus_Step2

data.name: Vendor_Asus_Step3

data.name: Vendor_Acer_Step1

data.name: Vendor_Acer_Step2
data.value: Go to the “Boot” tab and set “Secure Boot” to “Disabled”.

data.name: Vendor_Acer_Step4
data.value: Later, you can remove the password in the same menu by leaving it empty.
